structures.name: frontal bone
structures.definition: Forms the forehead and the roofs of the orbits.
structures.nursingNote: The anterior fontanelle lies where this bone meets the parietal bones; in infants a bulging fontanelle can signal raised intracranial pressure and a sunken one dehydration.
structures.medicineNote: Contains the frontal sinuses; the supraorbital notch or foramen transmits the supraorbital nerve and vessels.

structures.name: parietal bone
structures.definition: Paired bones forming the roof and upper sides of the cranium.
structures.nursingNote: Both fontanelles border these bones; palpate fontanelles with the infant calm and held upright.
structures.medicineNote: Joined to each other at the sagittal suture, to the frontal bone at the coronal suture and to the occipital bone at the lambdoid suture.

structures.name: temporal bone
structures.definition: Paired bones at the sides and base of the skull that house the ear.
structures.nursingNote: Tympanic thermometers read from the ear canal in this bone; pull the pinna up and back in adults, down and back in children under about 3.
structures.medicineNote: The petrous part houses the middle and inner ear; the pterion, where four bones meet, overlies the middle meningeal artery (extradural haematoma risk).

structures.name: occipital bone
structures.definition: Forms the back and base of the skull around the opening for the spinal cord.
structures.nursingNote: The back of the head is a high-risk pressure injury site in infants and immobile patients; the posterior fontanelle (with the parietal bones) closes by about 2 months.
structures.medicineNote: Contains the foramen magnum; the occipital condyles articulate with the atlas (C1) at the atlanto-occipital joint.

structures.name: sphenoid bone
structures.definition: Butterfly-shaped bone in the middle of the skull base, behind the eyes.
structures.nursingNote: After transsphenoidal pituitary surgery, patients should avoid blowing the nose and using straws; report clear nasal drainage, which may be cerebrospinal fluid.
structures.medicineNote: The sella turcica holds the pituitary gland; the optic canal and the foramina rotundum, ovale and spinosum pass through it.

structures.name: ethmoid bone
structures.definition: Light, spongy bone between the orbits that forms part of the nasal cavity roof.
structures.nursingNote: Its cribriform plate is thin; with a suspected base-of-skull fracture, avoid nasal tubes and nasopharyngeal airways and use the oral route.
structures.medicineNote: Olfactory nerve fibres pass through the cribriform plate; the perpendicular plate forms the upper nasal septum and the crista galli anchors the falx cerebri.

structures.name: nasal bone
structures.definition: Small paired bones forming the bridge of the nose.
structures.nursingNote: When passing a nasogastric tube, direct it straight back along the floor of the nose toward the ear, not upward toward the bridge.
structures.medicineNote: The most commonly fractured facial bones; they articulate with the frontal bone above and the frontal processes of the maxillae laterally.

structures.name: zygomatic bone
structures.definition: Paired bones forming the prominence of the cheek and part of the orbit wall.
structures.nursingNote: After facial trauma, a flattened cheek, periorbital swelling or numbness of the cheek can indicate a fracture here.
structures.medicineNote: Its temporal process joins the zygomatic process of the temporal bone to form the zygomatic arch; fractures can injure the infraorbital nerve.

structures.name: maxilla
structures.definition: Paired bone that holds the upper teeth and forms the front of the hard palate and the orbit floor.
structures.nursingNote: Upper teeth and dentures sit on its alveolar process; check the upper gums during oral care.
structures.medicineNote: Contains the maxillary sinus, the largest paranasal sinus; the infraorbital foramen lies just below the orbit.

structures.name: mandible
structures.definition: The only movable bone of the skull; it holds the lower teeth.
structures.nursingNote: A jaw thrust (lifting the angles of this bone forward) opens the airway without tilting the head in suspected spinal injury.
structures.medicineNote: Articulates at the temporomandibular joint; the inferior alveolar nerve enters at the mandibular foramen and exits as the mental nerve.

structures.name: cervical vertebrae
structures.definition: The seven bones of the neck, from the base of the skull to the shoulders.
structures.nursingNote: With suspected injury here, maintain manual in-line stabilisation and log-roll the patient; use a collar according to local protocol.
structures.medicineNote: C1 (atlas) has no body; C2 (axis) has the dens; transverse foramina carry the vertebral arteries; C7 is the vertebra prominens.

structures.name: thoracic vertebrae
structures.definition: The twelve spinal bones of the upper back that articulate with the ribs.
structures.nursingNote: Osteoporotic compression fractures here cause height loss and kyphosis; measure height routinely in older adults.
structures.medicineNote: Have costal facets for the ribs, heart-shaped bodies and long spinous processes that slope downward.

structures.name: lumbar vertebrae
structures.definition: The five largest movable vertebrae, in the lower back.
structures.nursingNote: Lumbar puncture is done at L3–L4 or L4–L5 with the patient curled up; a line between the top of the iliac crests crosses about L4.
structures.medicineNote: The spinal cord ends at about L1–L2 (conus medullaris), so needles below this level enter the cauda equina space.

structures.name: sacrum
structures.definition: Triangular bone of five fused vertebrae wedged between the hip bones.
structures.nursingNote: The skin over this bone is the most common site for pressure injuries; reposition immobile patients regularly and inspect it.
structures.medicineNote: The sacral promontory marks the pelvic inlet; the sacral hiatus is the entry point for caudal epidural anaesthesia.

structures.name: coccyx
structures.definition: Small triangular bone of fused rudimentary vertebrae at the base of the spine.
structures.nursingNote: Often bruised after falls onto the buttocks; pressure-relieving cushions help when sitting is painful.
structures.medicineNote: Usually three to five fused segments; it gives attachment to the gluteus maximus and the anococcygeal ligament.

structures.name: ribs
structures.definition: Twelve pairs of curved bones that form the cage around the thorax.
structures.nursingNote: Fractures here cause painful, shallow breathing and a risk of pneumonia; encourage deep breathing with good pain relief.
structures.medicineNote: Pairs 1–7 are true, 8–10 false and 11–12 floating; the neurovascular bundle runs in the costal groove, so chest drains pass just above a rib.

structures.name: sternum
structures.definition: Flat bone in the midline of the chest to which the upper ribs attach.
structures.nursingNote: Adult CPR compressions go on the lower half of this bone, 5–6 cm deep at 100–120 per minute.
structures.medicineNote: Made of the manubrium, body and xiphoid process; the sternal angle marks the 2nd costal cartilage and the T4–T5 level.

structures.name: clavicle
structures.definition: S-shaped bone running horizontally between the sternum and the shoulder.
structures.nursingNote: Subclavian central lines are inserted just below this bone; watch for signs of pneumothorax afterwards.
structures.medicineNote: The most commonly fractured bone, usually in the middle third; it is the first bone to start ossifying.

structures.name: scapula
structures.definition: Flat triangular bone on the upper back that forms the back of the shoulder.
structures.nursingNote: For a deltoid injection, find the acromion process of this bone and inject 2.5–5 cm (2–3 fingerbreadths) below it.
structures.medicineNote: Key landmarks are the spine, acromion, coracoid process and glenoid cavity; the inferior angle lies at about T7.

structures.name: humerus
structures.definition: The long bone of the upper arm, from shoulder to elbow.
structures.nursingNote: The greater tubercle at its upper end is an intraosseous (IO) access site in emergencies.
structures.medicineNote: Surgical neck fractures risk the axillary nerve; mid-shaft fractures risk the radial nerve in the radial groove.

structures.name: radius
structures.definition: Lateral bone of the forearm, on the thumb side.
structures.nursingNote: The radial pulse is felt at the wrist on the thumb side, over the lower end of this bone.
structures.medicineNote: Distal fractures after a fall on an outstretched hand (Colles fracture) are common; its head articulates with the capitulum at the elbow.

structures.name: ulna
structures.definition: Medial bone of the forearm, on the little-finger side, forming the point of the elbow.
structures.nursingNote: After forearm fractures or casting, check finger colour, warmth, capillary refill, sensation and movement (neurovascular observations).
structures.medicineNote: The olecranon forms the elbow tip and its trochlear notch grips the trochlea of the humerus.

structures.name: carpals
structures.definition: Eight small bones arranged in two rows that form the wrist.
structures.nursingNote: Snuffbox tenderness after a fall on an outstretched hand is treated as a suspected scaphoid fracture even if the first X-ray is normal.
structures.medicineNote: The scaphoid is the most often fractured; its blood supply enters distally, so proximal pole fractures risk avascular necrosis.

structures.name: metacarpals
structures.definition: Five long bones forming the palm, between the wrist and the fingers.
structures.nursingNote: The dorsal metacarpal veins on the back of the hand are common peripheral cannulation sites.
structures.medicineNote: A fracture of the fifth one's neck after punching is called a boxer's fracture.

structures.name: phalanges
structures.definition: The fourteen small bones of the fingers and thumb in each hand.
structures.nursingNote: Capillary refill and pulse oximetry are checked at the fingertips, over the distal bones of the fingers.
structures.medicineNote: Each finger has proximal, middle and distal bones; the thumb has only proximal and distal. The foot has its own set.

structures.name: medial epicondyle
structures.definition: Bony prominence on the inner side of the lower end of the humerus.
structures.nursingNote: The ulnar nerve runs just behind it (the 'funny bone'); pad elbows when positioning patients to avoid nerve compression.
structures.medicineNote: Common origin of the forearm flexors; inflammation here is medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow).

structures.name: lateral epicondyle
structures.definition: Bony prominence on the outer side of the lower end of the humerus.
structures.nursingNote: The antecubital fossa, the usual venepuncture site (median cubital vein), lies just below the line joining the two epicondyles.
structures.medicineNote: Common origin of the forearm extensors; overuse causes lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow).

structures.name: hip bone
structures.definition: Large paired bone made of the ilium, ischium and pubis, forming the side wall of the bony pelvic ring.
structures.nursingNote: Ventrogluteal injection: palm on the greater trochanter, index finger on the anterior superior iliac spine, middle finger along the iliac crest; inject in the centre of the V.
structures.medicineNote: The three parts fuse at the acetabulum; the two of them, with the sacrum and coccyx, form the bony pelvis.

structures.name: femur
structures.definition: The longest and strongest bone in the body, in the thigh.
structures.nursingNote: The vastus lateralis injection site is the middle third of the thigh, lateral to the front, between the greater trochanter and the knee; it is the preferred IM site in infants.
structures.medicineNote: Intracapsular neck fractures can disrupt the medial circumflex femoral artery and cause avascular necrosis of the head.

structures.name: patella
structures.definition: Small triangular bone at the front of the knee.
structures.nursingNote: The knee-jerk reflex is tested by tapping the tendon just below this bone.
structures.medicineNote: The largest sesamoid bone, embedded in the quadriceps tendon; it improves the leverage of knee extension.

structures.name: tibia
structures.definition: The larger, weight-bearing bone on the medial side of the lower leg.
structures.nursingNote: Its upper front surface, 1–2 cm below and medial to the tibial tuberosity, is a common intraosseous (IO) access site, especially in children.
structures.medicineNote: Its anteromedial surface lies just under the skin, so open fractures are common; its distal end forms the medial malleolus.

structures.name: fibula
structures.definition: The thin bone on the lateral side of the lower leg.
structures.nursingNote: The common fibular nerve wraps around its neck; tight casts or side-lying pressure can cause foot drop, so check ankle dorsiflexion.
structures.medicineNote: Its distal end forms the lateral malleolus of the ankle; it bears little body weight.

structures.name: tarsals
structures.definition: Seven bones forming the ankle and the back half of the foot.
structures.nursingNote: The dorsalis pedis pulse is felt on the top of the foot over these bones, just lateral to the big-toe extensor tendon.
structures.medicineNote: They are the talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid and three cuneiforms; the talus transmits body weight from the tibia.

structures.name: calcaneus
structures.definition: The largest tarsal bone, forming the heel.
structures.nursingNote: Newborn heel-prick samples are taken from the medial or lateral edge of the plantar heel, avoiding the centre to protect this bone.
structures.medicineNote: The calcaneal (Achilles) tendon inserts on its posterior surface; fractures from falls from height often come with lumbar spine fractures.
